To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
synchrotron radio emission from pre-main-sequence stars arises from the interaction of their magnetic fields and that this emission is a measure of the energy stored in the fields.

(1) a pre-main-sequence star's magnetospheric field interacts with its stellar companion's magnetospheric magnetic field, and (2) the resulting interaction energy, stored in the composite stellar magnetic field, is released as a burst of synchrotron emission near periastrons.

synchrotron emission from pre-main-sequence binaries is produced by the interaction between magnetic fields from the stars, and that the energy dissipated by the magnetic interaction is a small fraction of the energy available to the system.

the magnetic interactions of young stars in close binaries and their effects on the surrounding environment.
the physics of the interaction of two magnetic fields in close binary systems.
the interaction of magnetic fields in close binary systems, which can dissipate energy and produce synchronous radio emission.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the observed synchrotron emission from pre-main-sequence binaries is a consequence of magnetic interactions, not a sign of a new class of objects.
the observed radiation is a consequence of the magnetic interaction between the binary components, and not a consequence of the accretion process.
